articles.title: SoftBank junk bond sale raises stakes for CEOTOKYO — SoftBank’s promise to pay its highest-ever yields in a record $11 billion junk-bond offering highlights the pressure on CEO Masayoshi Son to secure returns on his all-in bet on AI amid concerns about possible overheating in the market. The SoftBank debt issuance last month added to a sharp surge in corporate borrowing this year, including major bond sales from Amazon.com, Alphabet and Tencent. The scale of Son’s investments, which include backing totaling $64.6 billion for ChatGPT maker OpenAI, in particular, has made the technology-and-investing conglomerate a bellwether for AI sentiment. Those fresh investments are now coming under sharper scrutiny by analysts and investors amid worries about the degree of concentration in SoftBank’s portfolio and whether a payoff from the expenditures by AI companies will come soon enough. SoftBank previously sold shares in Nvidia and T-Mobile US to fund its investments, but it is now borrowing at record yields of up to 9.75 percent in order to retain assets that it believes will appreciate, a senior SoftBank executive told Reuters. “We’ve borrowed money in large part because we don’t want to sell assets that we believe will keep rising in value,” said Alex Clavel, CEO of SoftBank Investment Advisers, which manages the Vision Funds. Sam Altman’s OpenAI is the core investment in the latest iteration of Son’s investment strategy, following lucrative bets on Chinese tech giant Alibaba and chip designer Arm “Given OpenAI’s appreciation to date, 9.75 percent is still very reasonable,” Clavel said. Arm’s valuation has grown fivefold since it floated in 2023 and further listings from SoftBank’s private AI portfolio would clarify their value and more easily allow the assets to be monetized for additional investment activity. Altman has said OpenAI will not go public this year, citing safety concerns about AI. It also faces competition from rival Anthropic and hyperscalers, as well as low-cost Chinese labs. SoftBank was previously “betting on a bunch of numbers at the roulette table. Now it’s red or black; either lose everything or gain everything,” MST Financial analyst David Gibson said. Increased scrutiny of AI-related fundraising SoftBank will pay its highest-ever coupon of 9.75 percent on a bond issued last month that matures in 2034. That return compares with Alphabet offering 5.2 percent for a bond issued in August that matures in 2033. SoftBank’s shares surged to a record high of 8,632 yen in June, though they have fallen 38 percent since then, while its credit default swap spreads jumped 24 percent over the same period. SoftBank’s higher yields reflect investor perceptions of their risk and concentration in large positions, analysts say. “The bets are much bigger than we’ve ever seen,” said Amir Anvarzadeh of Asymmetric Advisors, who recommends shorting the stock. James Athey, a fixed-income portfolio manager at Marlborough, said the fund was not allocating to high-yield bonds at this stage of the credit cycle, given current tight spread levels. “SoftBank is so aggressive, so concentrated and so all-in; I don’t think we’d be looking there first anyway,” he said. Clavel, however, says SoftBank’s OpenAI backing reflects their deep business ties. “We see OpenAI as a partner, building a relationship that can deliver strategic value as well as financial returns,” he said. reuters

articles.title: Canadian dollar touches an 18-month low as the US dollar jumps on hot CPI
articles.description: The US dollar is broadly stronger today and that briefly pushed it to the highest against the Canadian dollar since April 2025. The peak was 1.4299 (or 0.6993 CAD). The 70-cent level is a sensitive one domestically and a clean break of it could give Canadians another reason not to travel south this winter. The loonie had made strong gains yesterday as the post-jobs report weakness reversed. Friday's data saw Canada unexpectedly shed jobs but a closer look showed it was driven by government job losses in healthcare and education. The latter is a category that's particularly hard to seasonally adjust for in September due to school restarting while neither is indicative of underlying economic strength. That said, there have been mixed indications on the Canadian economy and the housing sector in much of the country appears to be in the midst of another leg down. Where it gets interesting is how central banks are reacting. In the year ahead, there are 97 basis points of hikes priced in for the Bank of Canada and 92 basis points for the Federal Reserve. Today's US CPI report narrowed that gap and if we see the Canadian economy stumble or the US accelerate further, then a real USD-positive divergence could open up. Note that the starting points are already highly divergent with the Fed at 3.75-4.00% and the Bank of Canada at 2.25%. That extends further out the curve where Treasuries are paying notably more than Government of Canada bonds. As for the USD/CAD chart, it's telling that it's pushing through the 2026 highs. That doesn't leave much in the way of resistance until the Liberation Day peaks in the 1.45-1.47 range come into play. USDCAD weekly: If we get into the mid-1.40s, I would be tempted to lean against that resistance as I expect the money to flow out of the US when the AI boom ebbs. A better trading relationship between Canada and the US could also turn the pair. In terms of the fundamentals, the Canadian dollar has been buffered by commodity prices. Unfortunately, the Western Canadian Select oil discount has blown out recently, meaning that Canadian producers largely won't be getting global prices for their crude. PM Carney announced a new pipeline to the west coast but it will take 5-10 years to build after the usual Canadian court challenges and litigation. For oil, the medium-term risks may be more to the downside if the US or Iran is forced to accept a peace in Hormuz. I tend to think the timelines for 'normalized' oil prices are long because of the extensive inventory rebuilding that will need to happen but any peace will be oil-negative for a time. In terms of consumers, spending has held up well in both places and RBC today is out with fresh Canadian cardholder data for September. They note that core sales rose 0.5% m/m led by discretionary categories. Entertainment and arts spending increased 1.4%, travel rose 1%, and dining grew a more modest 0.3%. High gasoline prices are obviously digging into budgets but so far they haven't cracked and that could give the Bank of Canada fodder to hike further from here. I'm skeptical that they will hike the four full hikes priced into the curve through 2027. This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

That was the message from Keo and Zels as they looked ahead to the opening round of the 2026-27 competition, with the Stormers hosting Bristol Bears, the Bulls welcoming Stade Français, and the 10bet Lions […] The post Investec Champions Cup is SA rugby’s next frontier appeared first on KEO.co.za.

articles.title: Building an AI data center costs billions. Defending it is another story
articles.description: Over four days last week, Ukrainian drones struck three data centers operated by Yandex, Russia’s largest technology company. Facilities went offline, disrupting services used by banks, retailers, and ordinary Russians. One of the sites, in Sasovo, housed tens of thousands of servers and two of the supercomputers used to develop Yandex’s AI models. The strikes followed Russian attacks on Ukraine’s own digital infrastructure, including one that left Kyiv’s Parkovyi Data Center so badly damaged that its operators said the facility could not be restored. The back-and-forth offers a glimpse of the damage that can be inflicted by attacking the physical infrastructure of the digital economy. And with governments and tech companies pouring billions into the data centers powering AI, including its growing military applications, the stakes are only getting higher. When I reported from Ukraine this summer, I saw how the country’s military was putting AI to work, from helping drones navigate without GPS to analyzing battlefield intelligence and recommending decisions to commanders. Many of those applications depend on powerful computing infrastructure—and that infrastructure, often housed in enormous buildings full of expensive computers, isn’t particularly hard to find. As the latest strikes show, it isn’t necessarily hard to hit, either. The problem with hiding data centers “If the Russians or the Chinese were using AI to accelerate their operations, I would definitely want to target those data centers,” says Jeffrey Lewis, a distinguished fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute and professor at the Middlebury Institute of International Studies. Lewis is particularly concerned about facilities handling AI inference, the process of running trained models. As militaries use AI to analyze intelligence and speed up decisions, the computing power behind those systems could become an inviting target in a major conflict. Good luck hiding a data center. These things are enormous, consume extraordinary amounts of electricity, and produce enough heat to require elaborate cooling systems. You could bury one underground, Lewis says, but that would be expensive, and it wouldn’t eliminate its dependence on power lines and communications links. “You can put the whole data center underground, but at some point there has to be a cable or an antenna that brings the data out,” he says. (Moving data centers into space, as several tech giants are now exploring, presents its own problems, namely that the satellites housing servers would also be vulnerable to attack, and a direct hit could create a debris field that threatens other spacecraft.) The risks haven’t gone unnoticed. A British government assessment warned of physical attacks and the risks of geographically concentrated facilities; a U.S. Government Accountability Office report identified the Pentagon’s Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability program as a mission-critical IT acquisition; and a House Armed Services Committee report called for an examination of the physical and cyber risks of putting commercial AI data centers on military installations. More recently, RAND researchers proposed a class of highly secure AI inference facilities, though their emphasis was on preventing theft or manipulation of models, rather than surviving drone strikes. The cost of a direct hit There’s an uncomfortable economic reality at play, too. Companies are spending billions to build data centers, but disabling them can require far less-expensive weapons. In March, Iranian drones struck Amazon Web Services facilities in the United Arab Emirates and damaged infrastructure in Bahrain. The strikes disrupted cloud services, and the effects have lingered. In September, AWS said it could not restore access to resources and data stored exclusively in one affected UAE availability zone or its Bahrain region. Customers with backups elsewhere had ways to recover; those without them faced the prospect of permanent losses. The attacks are prompting governments to reconsider where data centers belong, says Mehdi Paryavi, chairman and CEO of the International Data Center Authority. “We used to tell people, ‘Don’t build data centers near military targets,’” he says. “Now we’re telling people, ‘Don’t put military bases near data centers.’” Paryavi says governments around the world are asking his organization whether projects ought to move to safer locations. His preferred approach is to group facilities into a handful of so-called digital hubs, rather than trying to defend thousands of scattered sites. And sure, concentrating a country’s computing power in a few locations gives an adversary a much shorter list of places to attack, but Paryavi argues that those locations would be far easier to protect. “It’s impossible to secure 50,000 data centers around the country,” he says, “but it’s very easy to secure five locations.” The trouble with secrecy Then there’s the question of secrecy. Paryavi argues that publicizing data-center locations creates security risks, but concedes that people living near proposed sites have good reason to demand information about the power and water they’ll consume. “The community concerns are legitimate concerns that need to be addressed,” he says. And clearly, the risks to civilians extend well beyond power and water use. A strike on a data center could cause relatively few immediate casualties (the buildings are generally sparsely staffed), but the consequences could still prove quite dangerous, disrupting, for example, hospitals and emergency dispatch systems that depend on its computing power. The International Committee of the Red Cross warned earlier this year that data centers used by militaries may, depending on their function, become lawful military targets, even as the laws of war require attackers to account for harm to civilians who depend on the same infrastructure. As AI becomes increasingly important to military operations, the incentive to attack the infrastructure powering it will only grow. This is, Lewis argues, a fairly predictable consequence of technological progress, even if governments aren’t necessarily prepared for it. “When you discover something is valuable,” he says, “you then create the incentive for people to target it.”
